findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new constant references OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE but the diff adds no `import org.keycloak.OAuth2Constants;` to Constants.java (package org.keycloak.models, so OAuth2Constants is not resolvable without import), which fails compilation of server-spi-private. `mvn build` of server-spi-private fails with 'cannot find symbol: OAuth2Constants', blocking the entire change; the hunk adds only the constant lines and no import.

[BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher inverts the check (`if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`) so it returns false exactly when the grant shortcut MATCHES, and additionally slices substring(3,5) — the wrong 2-char window — instead of the grant-type chars at positions 4-5 (substring(4,6)). Every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion fails against correctly-issued tokens (matcher returns false on the matching shortcut) and, even after fixing the inversion, substring(3,5) grabs the last char of the token-type plus the first char of the grant shortcut, so 'ac' would compare 'tc'+'a' — the grant check never validates anything real.

[BUG] The constructor null-check block contains a copy-paste duplicate: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` appears twice while rawTokenId itself is never null-checked. A null rawTokenId slips past validation into the AccessTokenContext and later produces a token id like 'onrtna:null' via String concatenation in encodeTokenId instead of failing fast with the intended NPE, yielding a malformed but accepted token id.

[ADVISORY] Adding the abstract method getShortcut() to the public SPI interface OAuth2GrantTypeFactory is a source- and binary-incompatible change for every out-of-tree OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation. Any custom extension JAR shipping its own grant type (the documented extension point for OAuth2 grants) fails with AbstractMethodError at runtime on first invocation of the new encoder path after upgrading Keycloak, with no compile-time signal to the extension author.

[ADVISORY] The duplicate-shortcut validation compares only map sizes, so a collision where two grant factories both produce the (id, shortcut) pair of another entry (an id/shortcut swap between two grants) leaves sizes equal and the check passes silently. A deployer adding two custom grants whose id/shortcut pairs are crossed gets the wrong grant type decoded from token ids with no startup error; the validation message promises uniqueness detection it cannot fully deliver.

[ADVISORY] The test bypasses postInit by writing package-private fields grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts directly from a plain HashMap, so the ConcurrentHashMap creation, the provider-factory stream scan, and the duplicate-shortcut validation added in this diff are never executed by any test. A regression in postInit (e.g. the size-based collision check or the factory scan throwing for an unregistered grant) reaches production untested; when getShortcutByGrantType later refreshes maps it calls sessionFactory.getProviderFactory on the null sessionFactory for unknown grants, causing an NPE path no test covers.

[ADVISORY] Constants.GRANT_TYPE is set to the full grant name OAuth2Constants.TOKEN_EXCHANGE_GRANT_TYPE on the client session context only in exchangeClientToOIDCClient; sibling token-exchange code paths in this class (e.g. exchange client-to-SAML or the direct-exchange branches) leave the attribute unset, so those tokens encode grant shortcut 'na'. Tokens minted through the other token-exchange branches carry the UNKNOWN ('na') grant shortcut in their jti, so later consumers decoding the token id misclassify real token-exchange tokens as unknown-grant tokens.

[BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher's success condition is inverted: it returns false when the grant shortcut matches the expected value. Every valid token id (e.g. 'onrtcc:uuid' for client credentials) fails the matcher and every token with a wrong grant passes, so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertions assert the opposite of the diff's contract and will fail (or silently pass on wrong data).

[BUG] The matcher extracts the grant shortcut with items[0].substring(3, 5) but the encoder places the grant shortcut at indices 4-5 (sessionType 0-1, tokenType 2-3, grantType 4-5), contradicting the comment 'starts at character 4th char and is 2-chars long'. The matcher compares the expected grant shortcut against the last char of tokenType plus the first char of grantType, so even after fixing the inverted return it would never match a real token id; all four affected event assertions become dead checks.

[BUG] encodeTokenId never validates that the grant shortcut is exactly 2 characters, while getTokenContextFromTokenId hard-requires the prefix to be exactly 6 chars ('Expected length of 6'). A custom or newly deployed OAuth2GrantTypeFactory whose getShortcut() returns anything other than 2 chars (e.g. 'tok') causes the server to mint access tokens whose own ids its decoder then rejects with IllegalArgumentException during token validation/introspection, locking out all clients of that grant until tokens expire.

[BUG] The constructor null-checks grantType twice ('Null grantType not allowed' then 'Null rawTokenId not allowed' both passing grantType), so rawTokenId is never null-checked. A null rawTokenId is accepted by the constructor and encodeTokenId then concatenates the string 'null' into the token id ('onrtna:null'), producing a token id the decoder maps to literal rawId 'null' — a corrupted token id that no caller can correlate back to a real generated id.

[ADVISORY] The new abstract getShortcut() method is added directly to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface with no default implementation, breaking every out-of-tree custom grant implementation at class-loading time (AbstractMethodError / compile failure). Any Keycloak deployment with a custom OAuth2GrantType SPI extension fails to deploy or crashes on first use after upgrading; the interface should have provided a default (e.g. derive from getId or 'na') to preserve backward compatibility.

[ADVISORY] The public Context(Context) copy constructor is deleted, removing public API surface used by grant subclasses and external grant implementations that wrap or fork a context. Custom grant types extending OAuth2GrantType that call new Context(context) fail to compile/deploy, and the removal also silently drops grantType in any surviving copy path — an unflagged breaking SPI change in a file whose purpose is SPI stability.

[ADVISORY] The duplicate-shortcut/ID validation in postInit only compares map sizes, which fails to detect two grants sharing a shortcut only when they also share the id (impossible) but does detect collision — yet no test exercises this validation, and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest bypasses postInit entirely by hand-seeding the maps. The size-diff heuristic and the lazy map-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut (lines ~100-130, which dereference sessionFactory) are completely uncovered: DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest constructs the factory without postInit, so a regression in collision detection or in the hot-refresh lookup (e.g. a null sessionFactory in unit context) ships unnoticed; a real collision between two bundled grants would corrupt grant-type attribution in every token id.

[ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext — the encode-side core that reads persistence state, offline flag, lightweight-token flag and the GRANT_TYPE session attribute — has zero test coverage: DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest only tests decode/encode round-trips, and no integration test in this diff asserts the actual token-id format of a minted token end-to-end. A regression in mapping a session to sessionType/tokenType (e.g. misreading offline sessions as online, or AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken now being static and called with a session lacking a client in context, throwing NPE at session.getContext().getClient()) would ship green because nothing asserts the encoded ids of real grants; the AssertEvents matchers were the only end-to-end check and they are themselves broken.

[ADVISORY] testIncorrectGrantType catches RuntimeException instead of the specific IllegalArgumentException the decoder throws, so the assertion does not distinguish the intended validation error from any unrelated runtime failure in decode (e.g. NPE from a refactor). If the decode path is refactored to throw a different exception before reaching the grant-shortcut validation, the test still passes, hiding the loss of the validation contract on the token-validation hot path where a broken id currently surfaces as a 500 to token-refresh clients.

[BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher's success condition is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false (no-match) exactly when the grant shortcut matches the expected value, so expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectAuthReqIdToToken/expectDeviceCodeToToken all fail on correctly-encoded token IDs and pass only on wrong grant types. Every integration test asserting Details.TOKEN_ID via these helpers fails against a correctly working implementation, and a regression that encodes the wrong grant shortcut would be silently green, defeating the only end-to-end verification of the encoding.

[BUG] The matcher extracts the grant shortcut with `items[0].substring(3, 5)` (characters 3-4) although the encoder places the grant shortcut at characters 4-5 (`DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId` concatenates 2-char sessionType + 2-char tokenType + 2-char grantType, so the grant is substring(4,6)), contradicting the comment 'starts at character 4th char'. Even after fixing the inverted return, the matcher compares the expected grant shortcut against the last char of tokenType plus the first char of the grant shortcut, so expectCodeToToken("ac") would only pass when tokenType ends in 'a', producing wrong-grant false positives/negatives in all four event assertions.

[BUG] The constructor's null check for rawTokenId is a duplicated check of grantType (`Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")`), so rawTokenId is never validated for null despite the message naming it. A null rawTokenId (e.g., a caller passing a null generated id) is silently accepted and later renders as the string 'null' inside the encoded token id via encodeTokenId, corrupting every issued token's jti instead of failing fast with the intended NullPointerException.

[ADVISORY] The diff deletes the public copy-constructor `Context(Context context)` from a shipped SPI class in server-spi-private while adding the grantType field, changing the public surface without any requirement in the stated intent (grant-type context encoding) demanding it. Out-of-tree OAuth2GrantType implementations (and any SPI subclass) that used `new Context(otherContext)` to clone and enrich a context no longer compile against this version; the removal is unrelated API churn bundled into a feature PR, and grantType is silently dropped for anyone hand-rolling the field copy.

[ADVISORY] The import `org.keycloak.protocol.oidc.grants.TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory` is added but never used — the grant type is set via the string literal `OAuth2Constants.TOKEN_EXCHANGE_GRANT_TYPE` two lines below instead of the factory's constant. Dead import plus a parallel hand-maintained literal: if the token-exchange grant id string ever changes in TokenExchangeGrantTypeFactory.getId(), this site silently encodes the stale literal, and IDE unused-import warnings accumulate for the next editor of this file.

[ADVISORY] initToken unconditionally calls `session.getProvider(TokenContextEncoderProvider.class)` and encodes the id, but no consumer of the encoded context exists anywhere in this diff — getTokenContextFromTokenId has zero production call sites, making the token-id format change and the whole decode path ships-inert. Every access token issued by every realm gets a non-UUID id (`onrtrt:<uuid>`) with only the default provider able to read it, and nothing in the deployment uses the decoded information; any client or storage assuming UUID-shaped jti (logs, external claim validators, the still-UUID-expecting DETAIL matchers not updated in this diff) is exposed to the format change with no compensating consumer to justify it.

[BUG] The constructor validates grantType twice and never validates rawTokenId: the second line reads Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") — a copy-paste of the wrong variable. A null rawTokenId passes the constructor silently; the null-check the message promises is dead, and a null rawTokenId produces an encoded token id ending in ':' (e.g. "onrtac:") that getTokenContextFromTokenId then decodes with rawTokenId="" instead of failing fast as intended.

[BUG] isAccessTokenId inverts its match logic and reads the grant shortcut from the wrong index: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when the grant MATCHES, and substring(3,5) reads chars 3-4 (last char of tokenType + first char of grant) instead of chars 4-5 where the 2-char grant shortcut actually lives. The matcher accepts any "xxxxNN:uuid" id regardless of grant type — e.g. expectCodeToToken('ac') passes on a device-grant token — so all the AssertEvents assertions the diff rewrote (expectCodeToToken, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectAuthReqIdToToken) are vacuous stand-in guards that go green while the encoder writes the wrong grant shortcut; the integration suite can never catch a grant-mis-encoding regression.

[ADVISORY] grantType is captured once in the Context constructor from formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE), but setFormParams() can later swap the formParams object, leaving grantType stale from the original params. Any grant implementation that rewrites formParams before createTokenResponse (e.g. token-exchange-style request normalization) gets the pre-normalization grant_type baked into every token id's grant shortcut, so getTokenContextFromTokenId later reports the wrong grant for the token; the context silently disagrees with the request that actually produced it.

[ADVISORY] The public Context(Context) copy constructor is deleted in the same diff that adds a new field to Context, a breaking change to a published internal SPI. Out-of-tree grant-type providers that construct Context via the copy constructor fail to compile against this Keycloak version; since the SPI is advertised for custom grant extensions, every third-party grant built against the old API breaks on upgrade with no deprecation path.

[ADVISORY] The access token jti silently changes format from a bare UUID to "<2-char sessionType><2-char tokenType><2-char grant>:<uuid>", a sentinel-meaning-change for the public token contract with no versioning or compatibility claim. Clients, admin tooling, and external revocation/introspection integrations that pattern-match jti as a UUID (or persist it in a UUID-typed column) break at upgrade; revocation-by-token-id lookups keyed on the old format (e.g. stored revoked ids from before the upgrade) no longer compare equal to newly issued ids, so previously revoked tokens' id-matching is only preserved by coincidence of full-string storage.

[ADVISORY] The lazy map-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the two parallel ConcurrentHashMaps independently, and can leave them desynced: if a grant type's id was already mapped to a different shortcut, the refresh adds shortcut->name but the name->shortcut put overwrites the old binding, or vice versa, and the duplicate-shortcut invariant is only checked once in postInit. After a hot deploy of a new grant provider, a second lookup of the same grant can take the lazy path and write one map without the other (e.g. shortcut->name present, name->shortcut absent), so getTokenContextFromTokenId succeeds while encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException for the same grant on the next server — token issuance for that grant intermittently fails depending on which node handled which lookup.

[BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted logic and an off-by-one slice: it does `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — it rejects tokens whose grant shortcut matches and accepts tokens with a different grant, and even in corrected polarity substring(3,5) reads the wrong two characters (grant shortcut is at indices 4-5 of the 6-char prefix, so substring(4,6)). Every updated expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion passes for tokens issued with the wrong grant type and fails for correctly issued tokens, so the tests actively mask grant-encoding regressions instead of guarding them.

[BUG] The constructor checks `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, ...)` twice — the second call, intended to validate rawTokenId (message says "Null rawTokenId not allowed"), passes grantType again, so rawTokenId is never null-checked. A caller passing a null rawTokenId gets an AccessTokenContext built without error, and encodeTokenId then appends the string "null" to the token id (e.g. "onrtac:null"), producing access tokens whose jti fails UUID parsing in any consumer or revocation path that expects an id — the guard the author wrote is silently inert.

[ADVISORY] The public copy constructor `Context(Context)` is deleted while the class and its other public members remain in a published SPI-private API module, forcing out-of-tree OAuth2GrantType implementations that relied on the copy constructor to fail compilation, and any that recompile against the new constructor must now also supply form params or grantType stays null. Third-party grant-type extensions break at compile time (or, after recompiling against the new 13-arg constructor path, silently emit token ids with grant shortcut "na" because their form params never contained grant_type), and there is no deprecation cycle announcing the removal.

[BUG] getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext dereferences `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and then calls `userSession.getPersistenceState()` without a null check, but client-credential and other service-account flows can reach initToken with a client session whose user session lookup returns null depending on session provider state, and unlike the lightweight-token branch there is no fallback to UNKNOWN. A token-issuance request in that state throws NullPointerException from initToken, turning a previously working token grant into a 500 with no token returned.

[ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromTokenId treats any id without ':' as an old-format token and any 6-char prefix as parseable, but then throws IllegalArgumentException for unknown 2-char shortcuts, so a legacy UUID-format id happens to parse fine while a prefix from a future/deployed-away grant type is a hard failure at parse time rather than degrading to UNKNOWN. Consumers decoding a token issued under a grant type whose provider was later removed (undeployed extension) get IllegalArgumentException on getTokenContextFromTokenId, blocking revocation/introspection flows for still-valid tokens, whereas the design's own UNKNOWN sentinel shows graceful degradation was the intent for unrecognizable ids.

[BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher's grant-shortcut comparison is inverted: it returns false when the grant shortcut matches the expected value and true otherwise. `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` makes every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion pass only for tokens whose encoded grant type does NOT match the expected grant, so a token minted with the wrong grant-type context (e.g. an authorization-code token labeled 'rt') passes the suite and a token with the correct grant fails it, masking exactly the grant-context regressions this framework was built to catch.

[BUG] The constructor requires grantType twice and never null-checks rawTokenId: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`. A null rawTokenId is silently accepted, producing an AccessTokenContext whose encodeTokenId() emits a token id like 'onrtcc:' with an empty UUID suffix; downstream token-id parsers and the isUUID()-style validations in event assertions then fail or, worse, the empty id is stored/echoed in logs, while the copy-pasted check means the 'Null rawTokenId not allowed' guard never fires — the exact defect the message promises to prevent.

[ADVISORY] The new abstract getShortcut() method is added to the public OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI interface with no default implementation, while the factory casts every registered provider and calls it at startup. Any third-party or older deployment that ships its own OAuth2GrantTypeFactory jar against the previous interface gets an AbstractMethodError (or linkage failure) the moment DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit executes `(OAuth2GrantTypeFactory) factory1).getShortcut()` at server startup, turning a previously working extension into a hard boot failure on upgrade; a default like `return getId().substring(0,2)` would keep old providers alive.

[ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromTokenId throws IllegalArgumentException for any 6-char-prefix token id whose shortcut components are unrecognized (including prefixes containing ':'), and this id is attacker-influenced wherever a raw jti string crosses an API boundary before signature verification. Any code path that decodes context from a token id supplied by a client before the JWT signature is verified (e.g. revocation or introspection plumbing that reads the id string directly) turns a malformed 6-char-prefixed id into an unhandled IllegalArgumentException/500 rather than a clean 4xx/invalid-token rejection; if all decode sites operate on signature-verified tokens this never triggers, which is the author's rebuttal, but no such ordering is enforced or documented by the provider contract.

[ADVISORY] Making getShouldUseLightweightToken a public static utility that dereferences session.getContext().getClient() without a null check invites NPEs from the new call site in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext. initToken is invoked on paths (and by future SPI callers of the now-public static method) where session.getContext().getClient() is not guaranteed — e.g. session-context lookups triggered from a client-less request context — producing an NPE that fails token issuance with a 500; previously the method was package-private and only reachable from code paths that had already established the client.

[ADVISORY] The lazy cache-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the shared ConcurrentHashMaps with unvalidated values (factory.getShortcut() may be null or collide with an existing shortcut) and only the postInit path performs the duplicate-shortcut size check. A grant factory hot-deployed after startup whose getShortcut() returns null or collides with an existing entry is written into the caches without the collision validation, so getTokenContextFromTokenId silently misattributes one grant type's tokens to another grant — the size check that would catch this only runs at postInit and never again.

[BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher's comparison logic is inverted: it returns false (no match) exactly when the grant-type shortcut equals the expected shortcut. matchesSafely does `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — every integration test using expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken will FAIL when the token ID encoding is correct (grant shortcut present at chars 4–5), and will PASS when the encoded grant is wrong. The suite actively asserts the opposite of the intended behavior, so a regression that encodes the wrong grant shortcut goes undetected while correct code is flagged red.

[ADVISORY] isAccessTokenId never asserts the sessionType or tokenType portions of the encoded ID, verifying only the grant shortcut and UUID-ness of the raw id. A regression that flips the SessionType encoding (e.g. always encoding 'tr' for online sessions, or encoding UNKNOWN/'un') passes all event-based integration tests, because the matcher ignores characters 0–3 of the context segment. Checked the diff for tests asserting session-type encoding: only DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest (encode/decode roundtrips) and this matcher exist, neither covers SessionType/TokenType in a live flow.

[ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext — the new branch logic distinguishing TRANSIENT/OFFLINE/ONLINE sessions, lightweight-vs-regular token selection, and the null-grantType fallback to "na" — has no test anywhere in the diff. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest only exercises getTokenContextFromTokenId/encodeTokenId (decode direction); I scanned the diff's test files (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest.java, AssertEvents.java) and neither constructs a ClientSessionContext or asserts the ONLINE/OFFLINE/TRANSIENT classification. A misclassification (e.g. userSession.getPersistenceState() null NPE, or isOffline() checked before TRANSIENT) silently encodes wrong session type into every issued token's jti, and no test fails. This method is the only producer of encoded IDs in production (called from TokenManager.initToken), so a regression breaks every token ID.

[BUG] The constructor's fourth null check validates the wrong field: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` duplicates the grantType check instead of checking rawTokenId. rawTokenId can be passed as null without any exception, and the assertion's message misattributes it to grantType; a caller passing a null raw id gets an AccessTokenContext whose encodeTokenId() emits e.g. "onrtna:null", producing a token ID whose raw segment is the literal string "null" — and the existing test suite never passes a null rawTokenId, so nothing catches it.

[ADVISORY] The test's @Before hand-builds the factory's grant maps instead of calling postInit, so the duplicate-shortcut validation in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit (the map-size check that guards against two grants sharing a shortcut) is never exercised by any test. A future grant factory returning a colliding shortcut (e.g. two grants both using "ac") passes every test — postInit's IllegalStateException at factory startup is dead code from the suite's perspective, and the collision would only surface as tokens from two different grants decoding to the wrong grant type in production. Also, the runtime class-path (CIBA, device, UMA, token-exchange, authorization-code grants) is wider than the three-entry map the test wires, so the decode paths for shortcuts like "ac" are never tested.

[BUG] isAccessTokenId has an inverted return and a wrong substring offset, so it never actually validates the grant shortcut. The line `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when the grant MATCHES (inverted), and substring(3,5) reads the wrong characters anyway (the grant shortcut lives at chars 4-5, i.e. substring(4,6) — chars 3-4 are the tail of the token-type shortcut plus first grant char). Net effect: for any well-formed encoded id like 'onrtac' with expected 'ac', substring(3,5)='ta' != 'ac', the early return is skipped, and the matcher reduces to isUUID() on items[1] — every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion silently stops verifying the encoded grant context, so a regression that encodes the wrong grant type passes the whole suite.

[ADVISORY] Adding the abstract method getShortcut() to the public OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI is a breaking interface change with no default implementation, so already-compiled custom grant-type providers in the field fail at runtime. Any Keycloak deployment running a third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory (a supported extension point) upgraded to this version has its provider factory invoked in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit (gtf.getShortcut()), which throws AbstractMethodError because the deployed jar predates the method — a hard, unrecoverable startup failure of the whole server, not a per-request error, with no feature flag or migration note to disable it. Ship it with `default String getShortcut() { return "na"; }` or a config override to make the transition reversible.

[ADVISORY] All access tokens issued before this deploy (plain-UUID jti) decode to SessionType.UNKNOWN/TokenType.UNKNOWN/grantType 'na', and any later re-encode of that context throws, so pre-upgrade tokens are a permanently distinct class during and after rollout. During a rolling deploy and for the full remaining lifetime of pre-upgrade refresh/offline tokens (offline tokens can outlive the upgrade by design), getTokenContextFromTokenId returns UNKNOWN context; callers branching on the decoded context treat every legacy token as unknown, and encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException if such a context is ever re-encoded (e.g. a custom TokenContextEncoderProvider or future caller passing a decoded legacy context through encodeTokenId) — there is no documented one-way-door analysis for this data-format transition even though legacy tokens cannot be 'migrated' client-side.

[BUG] isAccessTokenId has inverted match logic: it returns false (no match) when the grant shortcut EQUALS the expected value and true when it differs. Every expected token ID with the correct grant prefix fails the matcher and every token ID with the WRONG grant passes, so the test asserts the opposite of its contract; grant-type regressions in token IDs go undetected and correct tokens cause spurious test failures.

[BUG] The constructor calls requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") twice instead of checking rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId passes validation. A null rawTokenId (e.g., from a caller passing the result of a failed ID generation) is accepted at construction and only surfaces later as an NPE deep inside JWT ID serialization on the token endpoint, producing a raw 500 instead of failing fast at the context boundary.

[ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromTokenId hard-assumes the encoded context prefix is exactly 6 chars (2+2+2), but the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() javadoc explicitly permits 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', so any custom grant with a non-2-char shortcut produces token IDs whose decode always throws IllegalArgumentException (and encode produces a prefix that fails its own round-trip). A third-party grant deployer following the interface javadoc gets every issued access token rejected at introspection/validation with 'Incorrect token id ... Expected length of 6' — a hard runtime failure with no startup-time validation of shortcut lengths.

[ADVISORY] postInit puts factory.getShortcut() into a ConcurrentHashMap with no null/length check, so a custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory returning a null shortcut triggers a NullPointerException during postInit — a hard server startup failure. An operator deploying an existing grant-type extension whose getShortcut() returns null (the interface contract does not forbid it) gets an NPE at Keycloak boot with no pointer to the offending provider, instead of a clear validation error naming the grant.

[ADVISORY] The lazy shortcut-map refresh in getShortcutByGrantType writes to grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts concurrently from request threads via ConcurrentHashMap, but the duplicate-shortcut invariant checked once in postInit (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()) is never re-validated on the lazy path, and a newly hot-deployed grant reusing an existing shortcut silently overwrites the earlier mapping. After a hot deploy of a grant with a colliding shortcut, tokens minted under one grant type decode as the other grant type — silently wrong token context reported to any consumer of getTokenContextFromTokenId, with no error logged or thrown.

In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.

Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.

Clients, admin tooling, and external revocation/introspection integrations that pattern-match jti as a UUID (or persist it in a UUID-typed column) break at upgrade; revocation-by-token-id lookups keyed on the old format (e.g. stored revoked ids from before the upgrade) no longer compare equal to newly issued ids, so previously revoked tokens' id-matching is only preserved by coincidence of full-string storage.

adjudication.rationale: The diff verifiably changes the access token `jti`/ID format: `TokenManager.initToken` no longer sets `token.id(KeycloakModelUtils.generateId())` but instead encodes a context prefix and appends `':' + rawTokenId` via `TokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId(...)` (e.g., `onrtcc:<uuid>`). Tests were updated to expect this new shape (`AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId(...)`), confirming the behavioral change. While this is not necessarily an implementation defect, it is a breaking public-contract/compatibility concern for any external tooling or clients that assume `jti` is a bare UUID; the diff shows no explicit versioning/compatibility signaling beyond the internal SPI.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The lazy map-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType/getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the two parallel ConcurrentHashMaps independently, and can leave them desynced: if a grant type's id was already mapped to a different shortcut, the refresh adds shortcut->name but the name->shortcut put overwrites the old binding, or vice versa, and the duplicate-shortcut invariant is only checked once in postInit. After a hot deploy of a new grant provider, a second lookup of the same grant can take the lazy path and write one map without the other (e.g. shortcut->name present, name->shortcut absent), so getTokenContextFromTokenId succeeds while encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException for the same grant on the next server — token issuance for that grant intermittently fails depending on which node handled which lookup.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show two parallel `ConcurrentHashMap`s (`grantsByShortcuts` and `grantsToShortcuts`) in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory` that are mutated via non-atomic paired `put` operations in the lazy refresh paths (`getShortcutByGrantType` / `getGrantTypeByShortcut`). However, the specific failure mode claimed (“write one map without the other”, leading to `getTokenContextFromTokenId` succeeding while `encodeTokenId` throws) is not directly supported by the shown code because both lazy paths always execute both `put`s in the same control flow when a factory is found. A real, diff-grounded concern remains: the lazy refresh can overwrite existing bindings without removing stale reverse entries or re-validating shortcut uniqueness (the duplicate-shortcut check runs only in `postInit`), which could lead to inconsistent bidirectional mappings after dynamic provider changes, but the described intermittent issuance failure is overstated/insufficiently verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher has inverted logic and an off-by-one slice: it does `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — it rejects tokens whose grant shortcut matches and accepts tokens with a different grant, and even in corrected polarity substring(3,5) reads the wrong two characters (grant shortcut is at indices 4-5 of the 6-char prefix, so substring(4,6)). Every updated expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion passes for tokens issued with the wrong grant type and fails for correctly issued tokens, so the tests actively mask grant-encoding regressions instead of guarding them.

adjudication.rationale: In AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId the matcher rejects correct grant shortcuts due to inverted condition: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when it matches. Also, based on the new token-id encoding (2 chars sessionType + 2 chars tokenType + 2 chars grant shortcut before `:`), the grant shortcut occupies indices [4,6), not [3,5), so `substring(3,5)` is off by one and spans tokenType/grantType. This makes the updated expectations (e.g., expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/etc.) validate the wrong thing and can pass for incorrect grants while failing for correct ones.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The constructor checks `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, ...)` twice — the second call, intended to validate rawTokenId (message says "Null rawTokenId not allowed"), passes grantType again, so rawTokenId is never null-checked. A caller passing a null rawTokenId gets an AccessTokenContext built without error, and encodeTokenId then appends the string "null" to the token id (e.g. "onrtac:null"), producing access tokens whose jti fails UUID parsing in any consumer or revocation path that expects an id — the guard the author wrote is silently inert.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext dereferences `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and then calls `userSession.getPersistenceState()` without a null check, but client-credential and other service-account flows can reach initToken with a client session whose user session lookup returns null depending on session provider state, and unlike the lightweight-token branch there is no fallback to UNKNOWN. adjudication.rationale: In `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext`, the code unconditionally does `UserSessionModel userSession = clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession();` and immediately calls `userSession.getPersistenceState()` / `userSession.isOffline()` with no null check. Since `TokenManager.initToken` now always derives the token id via `encoder.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext(clientSessionCtx, ...)`, any scenario where `getUserSession()` can be null would now NPE during token issuance. The diff itself shows the missing null-handling, but it does not prove from the diff alone that `getUserSession()` is actually nullable for client-credentials/service-account flows in practice.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromTokenId treats any id without ':' as an old-format token and any 6-char prefix as parseable, but then throws IllegalArgumentException for unknown 2-char shortcuts, so a legacy UUID-format id happens to parse fine while a prefix from a future/deployed-away grant type is a hard failure at parse time rather than degrading to UNKNOWN. Consumers decoding a token issued under a grant type whose provider was later removed (undeployed extension) get IllegalArgumentException on getTokenContextFromTokenId, blocking revocation/introspection flows for still-valid tokens, whereas the design's own UNKNOWN sentinel shows graceful degradation was the intent for unrecognizable ids.

adjudication.rationale: In DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId, any token id containing ':' with a 6-char prefix is parsed into 2-char shortcuts, and if any shortcut is unrecognized (session type/token type/grant type), it throws IllegalArgumentException (e.g., `if (gt == null) { throw ... }`). The code only degrades to UNKNOWN when there is no ':' (treated as “old token”) or when grantType attribute is null during encoding; it does not degrade to UNKNOWN for unknown shortcuts. This makes decoding brittle for tokens whose 2-char grant shortcut is not present in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory’s maps (e.g., if a grant provider was removed), which is the core of the finding. However, the claimed impact on revocation/introspection flows is not directly verifiable from the diff because no consumers of getTokenContextFromTokenId are shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher's grant-shortcut comparison is inverted: it returns false when the grant shortcut matches the expected value and true otherwise. `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` makes every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion pass only for tokens whose encoded grant type does NOT match the expected grant, so a token minted with the wrong grant-type context (e.g. an authorization-code token labeled 'rt') passes the suite and a token with the correct grant fails it, masking exactly the grant-context regressions this framework was built to catch.

adjudication.rationale: In AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId(), the matcher explicitly returns false when the extracted shortcut equals the expected shortcut: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, inverting the intended condition. Both issues are directly visible in the diff and would break the test assertions’ correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The constructor requires grantType twice and never null-checks rawTokenId: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed");`. A null rawTokenId is silently accepted, producing an AccessTokenContext whose encodeTokenId() emits a token id like 'onrtcc:' with an empty UUID suffix; downstream token-id parsers and the isUUID()-style validations in event assertions then fail or, worse, the empty id is stored/echoed in logs, while the copy-pasted check means the 'Null rawTokenId not allowed' guard never fires — the exact defect the message promises to prevent.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AccessTokenContext` constructor, the last null-check is clearly wrong: it calls `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` instead of checking `rawTokenId`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new abstract getShortcut() method is added to the public OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI interface with no default implementation, while the factory casts every registered provider and calls it at startup. Any third-party or older deployment that ships its own OAuth2GrantTypeFactory jar against the previous interface gets an AbstractMethodError (or linkage failure) the moment DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit executes `(OAuth2GrantTypeFactory) factory1).getShortcut()` at server startup, turning a previously working extension into a hard boot failure on upgrade; a default like `return getId().substring(0,2)` would keep old providers alive.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromTokenId throws IllegalArgumentException for any 6-char-prefix token id whose shortcut components are unrecognized (including prefixes containing ':'), and this id is attacker-influenced wherever a raw jti string crosses an API boundary before signature verification. Any code path that decodes context from a token id supplied by a client before the JWT signature is verified (e.g. revocation or introspection plumbing that reads the id string directly) turns a malformed 6-char-prefixed id into an unhandled IllegalArgumentException/500 rather than a clean 4xx/invalid-token rejection; if all decode sites operate on signature-verified tokens this never triggers, which is the author's rebuttal, but no such ordering is enforced or documented by the provider contract.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId()` throws `IllegalArgumentException` for certain attacker-controlled-looking inputs (e.g., 6-char context with unknown session/token/grant shortcuts, or wrong prefix length) rather than returning an `UNKNOWN` context (see `throw new IllegalArgumentException(...)` branches). However, the finding’s security impact claim depends on there being code paths that decode a client-supplied token id *before* JWT signature verification; no such call sites are shown in this diff, so the “turns into 500” part is not verifiable here. Also, the mention of “including prefixes containing ':'” is not supported by the implementation, which splits on the first `:` and treats everything before it as `encodedContext`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Making getShouldUseLightweightToken a public static utility that dereferences session.getContext().getClient() without a null check invites NPEs from the new call site in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext. initToken is invoked on paths (and by future SPI callers of the now-public static method) where session.getContext().getClient() is not guaranteed — e.g. session-context lookups triggered from a client-less request context — producing an NPE that fails token issuance with a 500; previously the method was package-private and only reachable from code paths that had already established the client.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(KeycloakSession)` `public static` and it still unconditionally dereferences `session.getContext().getClient().getAttribute(...)` with no null check. The new code path `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext(...)` calls this static method (`AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`), even though it already has `ClientSessionContext` available and does not ensure `session.getContext().getClient()` is set. This is a concrete robustness/edge-case concern introduced by the diff (potential NPE or using the wrong client context), but the diff alone doesn’t prove an actual execution path where the client is null, so it’s not a definitively verifiable defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The lazy cache-refresh paths in getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the shared ConcurrentHashMaps with unvalidated values (factory.getShortcut() may be null or collide with an existing shortcut) and only the postInit path performs the duplicate-shortcut size check. A grant factory hot-deployed after startup whose getShortcut() returns null or collides with an existing entry is written into the caches without the collision validation, so getTokenContextFromTokenId silently misattributes one grant type's tokens to another grant — the size check that would catch this only runs at postInit and never again.

adjudication.rationale: In DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory, the lazy refresh logic in getShortcutByGrantType() and getGrantTypeByShortcut() mutates the shared ConcurrentHashMaps without any validation. Specifically, getShortcutByGrantType() does `String shortcut = factory.getShortcut(); grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType); grantsToShortcuts.put(grantType, shortcut);` with no null/duplicate check. ConcurrentHashMap does not permit null keys/values, so a hot-deployed OAuth2GrantTypeFactory returning null shortcut would cause a runtime NPE. Also, if a newly deployed factory returns a shortcut that collides with an existing one, the `put` overwrites the existing mapping, potentially making getGrantTypeByShortcut() resolve that shortcut to the wrong grant type (silent misattribution). The only duplicate detection (`if (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size())`) runs in postInit() and is not re-run after these lazy updates.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The isAccessTokenId matcher's comparison logic is inverted: it returns false (no match) exactly when the grant-type shortcut equals the expected shortcut. matchesSafely does `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` — every integration test using expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken will FAIL when the token ID encoding is correct (grant shortcut present at chars 4–5), and will PASS when the encoded grant is wrong. The suite actively asserts the opposite of the intended behavior, so a regression that encodes the wrong grant shortcut goes undetected while correct code is flagged red.

adjudication.rationale: In AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId.matchesSafely, the grant-shortcut check is inverted: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` rejects exactly the expected shortcut and accepts mismatches (subject only to UUID check on the raw id). Additionally, based on the new token-id encoding (2 chars sessionType + 2 chars tokenType + 2 chars grant shortcut, see DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId), the grant shortcut should be at indices (4,6) of the 6-char prefix, not (3,5). This will cause integration assertions to behave opposite of intent and/or be unreliable.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] isAccessTokenId never asserts the sessionType or tokenType portions of the encoded ID, verifying only the grant shortcut and UUID-ness of the raw id. A regression that flips the SessionType encoding (e.g. always encoding 'tr' for online sessions, or encoding UNKNOWN/'un') passes all event-based integration tests, because the matcher ignores characters 0–3 of the context segment. Checked the diff for tests asserting session-type encoding: only DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest (encode/decode roundtrips) and this matcher exist, neither covers SessionType/TokenType in a live flow.

adjudication.rationale: Grounded in the diff: the new integration-test matcher `AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId` only inspects a 2-char slice of the pre-`:` context segment and then validates UUID-ness of the raw ID (`return isUUID().matches(items[1]);`), and it does not assert the first 4 characters that encode `SessionType` and `TokenType` (per `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId`, where st=substring(0,2) and tt=substring(2,4)). As the finding states, this means event-based integration tests would not catch regressions in session/token type encoding; only `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest` exercises session/token type roundtrips, not a live flow. This is a specific, diff-created test coverage gap around newly introduced token-id encoding logic (and thus important), but it is not itself a production defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext — the new branch logic distinguishing TRANSIENT/OFFLINE/ONLINE sessions, lightweight-vs-regular token selection, and the null-grantType fallback to "na" — has no test anywhere in the diff. DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest only exercises getTokenContextFromTokenId/encodeTokenId (decode direction); I scanned the diff's test files (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest.java, AssertEvents.java) and neither constructs a ClientSessionContext or asserts the ONLINE/OFFLINE/TRANSIENT classification. A misclassification (e.g. userSession.getPersistenceState() null NPE, or isOffline() checked before TRANSIENT) silently encodes wrong session type into every issued token's jti, and no test fails. This method is the only producer of encoded IDs in production (called from TokenManager.initToken), so a regression breaks every token ID.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds non-trivial production logic in `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext(...)` (classifying `UserSessionModel` into TRANSIENT/OFFLINE/ONLINE, choosing LIGHTWEIGHT vs REGULAR via `AbstractOIDCProtocolMapper.getShouldUseLightweightToken(session)`, and defaulting `grantType` to `UNKNOWN`/"na"). This method is then used in production from `TokenManager.initToken()` to build/encode the access token `jti`. The only new unit test (`DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest`) exercises `getTokenContextFromTokenId(...)` and `encodeTokenId(...)` (decode/roundtrip) and does not construct a `ClientSessionContext` or validate the session-type/token-type/grant-type derivation path. So the finding about missing tests for this new branch logic is accurate and specific to the diff, but it’s not itself a verifiable functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The constructor's fourth null check validates the wrong field: `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` duplicates the grantType check instead of checking rawTokenId. rawTokenId can be passed as null without any exception, and the assertion's message misattributes it to grantType; a caller passing a null raw id gets an AccessTokenContext whose encodeTokenId() emits e.g. "onrtna:null", producing a token ID whose raw segment is the literal string "null" — and the existing test suite never passes a null rawTokenId, so nothing catches it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test's @Before hand-builds the factory's grant maps instead of calling postInit, so the duplicate-shortcut validation in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit (the map-size check that guards against two grants sharing a shortcut) is never exercised by any test. A future grant factory returning a colliding shortcut (e.g. two grants both using "ac") passes every test — postInit's IllegalStateException at factory startup is dead code from the suite's perspective, and the collision would only surface as tokens from two different grants decoding to the wrong grant type in production. Also, the runtime class-path (CIBA, device, UMA, token-exchange, authorization-code grants) is wider than the three-entry map the test wires, so the decode paths for shortcuts like "ac" are never tested.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() builds grant shortcut maps from all OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations and validates uniqueness via a map-size check, throwing IllegalStateException on duplicates. However, DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderTest.before() does not call postInit() and instead manually populates factory.grantsByShortcuts with only "ro", "cc", and "na", then derives grantsToShortcuts. As a result, the duplicate-shortcut validation and the real runtime set of shortcuts (e.g., "ac", "rt", "ci", "dg", etc. added in this diff) are not exercised by tests, leaving a gap in coverage for collisions and decoding of those shortcuts.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] isAccessTokenId has an inverted return and a wrong substring offset, so it never actually validates the grant shortcut. The line `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;` returns false when the grant MATCHES (inverted), and substring(3,5) reads the wrong characters anyway (the grant shortcut lives at chars 4-5, i.e. substring(4,6) — chars 3-4 are the tail of the token-type shortcut plus first grant char). Net effect: for any well-formed encoded id like 'onrtac' with expected 'ac', substring(3,5)='ta' != 'ac', the early return is skipped, and the matcher reduces to isUUID() on items[1] — every expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken assertion silently stops verifying the encoded grant context, so a regression that encodes the wrong grant type passes the whole suite.
matched_golden_ids: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate issue describes the same bug: in isAccessTokenId the grant shortcut substring uses the wrong indices (should be substring(4,6) for chars 4–5) and the equality check’s return is inverted (it returns false when the grant matches, rather than returning true when combined with UUID validation).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Adding the abstract method getShortcut() to the public OAuth2GrantTypeFactory SPI is a breaking interface change with no default implementation, so already-compiled custom grant-type providers in the field fail at runtime. Any Keycloak deployment running a third-party OAuth2GrantTypeFactory (a supported extension point) upgraded to this version has its provider factory invoked in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit (gtf.getShortcut()), which throws AbstractMethodError because the deployed jar predates the method — a hard, unrecoverable startup failure of the whole server, not a per-request error, with no feature flag or migration note to disable it. Ship it with `default String getShortcut() { return "na"; }` or a config override to make the transition reversible.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new abstract method `String getShortcut()` to the public interface `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` (server-spi-private), with no default implementation. In `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit`, it iterates all `OAuth2GrantType` provider factories and unconditionally calls `gtf.getShortcut()`. Any already-compiled third-party implementation of `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` built against the previous interface would not have that method, so the call site can trigger `AbstractMethodError` at startup when loading provider factories, causing hard failure. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] All access tokens issued before this deploy (plain-UUID jti) decode to SessionType.UNKNOWN/TokenType.UNKNOWN/grantType 'na', and any later re-encode of that context throws, so pre-upgrade tokens are a permanently distinct class during and after rollout. During a rolling deploy and for the full remaining lifetime of pre-upgrade refresh/offline tokens (offline tokens can outlive the upgrade by design), getTokenContextFromTokenId returns UNKNOWN context; callers branching on the decoded context treat every legacy token as unknown, and encodeTokenId throws IllegalStateException if such a context is ever re-encoded (e.g. a custom TokenContextEncoderProvider or future caller passing a decoded legacy context through encodeTokenId) — there is no documented one-way-door analysis for this data-format transition even though legacy tokens cannot be 'migrated' client-side.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly introduces a new access-token ID format with a context prefix (DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId builds `st+tt+gt+':' + rawId`, and TokenManager.initToken now sets `token.id(encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx))`). For legacy tokens whose ID has no `:`, getTokenContextFromTokenId explicitly returns `SessionType.UNKNOWN`/`TokenType.UNKNOWN` and grantType `na` (see `if (indexOf == -1) { return new AccessTokenContext(...UNKNOWN..., UNKNOWN, UNKNOWN, encodedTokenId); }`). The provider also intentionally throws on re-encoding UNKNOWN session/token types (`encodeTokenId` throws IllegalStateException), and the new unit test `testOldToken` asserts this behavior. However, the finding’s broader claim about “callers branching on the decoded context” causing broken behavior during rolling upgrades is not directly verifiable from this diff, since no such branching usage is shown here. What is verifiable is the one-way format transition and the deliberate inability to re-encode decoded legacy context, which is a legitimate rollout/compatibility concern rather than a proven defect in this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] isAccessTokenId has inverted match logic: it returns false (no match) when the grant shortcut EQUALS the expected value and true when it differs. Every expected token ID with the correct grant prefix fails the matcher and every token ID with the WRONG grant passes, so the test asserts the opposite of its contract; grant-type regressions in token IDs go undetected and correct tokens cause spurious test failures.

adjudication.rationale: In AssertEvents.isAccessTokenId(), matchesSafely() contains `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`, which rejects the token when the extracted grant shortcut equals the expected value and otherwise proceeds to UUID match. This inverts the intended logic (it should fail when NOT equal). Additionally, given the new token-id format (2 chars sessionType + 2 chars tokenType + 2 chars grantType), the grant shortcut should start at index 4 (substring(4,6)), not (3,5), further breaking correctness.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The constructor calls requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed") twice instead of checking rawTokenId, so a null rawTokenId passes validation. A null rawTokenId (e.g., from a caller passing the result of a failed ID generation) is accepted at construction and only surfaces later as an NPE deep inside JWT ID serialization on the token endpoint, producing a raw 500 instead of failing fast at the context boundary.

adjudication.rationale: In `AccessTokenContext` constructor, the last validation line mistakenly calls `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` instead of checking `rawTokenId` (diff shows `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, ...)` twice). This means `rawTokenId` can be null and pass construction, contradicting the apparent intent and allowing an invalid context/token id to be created later.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getTokenContextFromTokenId hard-assumes the encoded context prefix is exactly 6 chars (2+2+2), but the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() javadoc explicitly permits 'usually like 3-letters shortcut', so any custom grant with a non-2-char shortcut produces token IDs whose decode always throws IllegalArgumentException (and encode produces a prefix that fails its own round-trip). A third-party grant deployer following the interface javadoc gets every issued access token rejected at introspection/validation with 'Incorrect token id ... Expected length of 6' — a hard runtime failure with no startup-time validation of shortcut lengths.

adjudication.rationale: In DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId(), the decoder hard-requires the prefix before ':' to be exactly 6 chars (2 for sessionType + 2 for tokenType + 2 for grantType) and throws IllegalArgumentException otherwise ("Expected length of 6."). But OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()’s new javadoc explicitly allows shortcuts that are “usually like 3-letters”, i.e., not guaranteed to be 2 chars. encodeTokenId() concatenates the grant shortcut without enforcing length, so any non-2-char shortcut would produce token IDs that the decoder cannot parse/round-trip. The factory’s postInit() validates uniqueness of shortcuts but does not validate shortcut length.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] postInit puts factory.getShortcut() into a ConcurrentHashMap with no null/length check, so a custom OAuth2GrantTypeFactory returning a null shortcut triggers a NullPointerException during postInit — a hard server startup failure. An operator deploying an existing grant-type extension whose getShortcut() returns null (the interface contract does not forbid it) gets an NPE at Keycloak boot with no pointer to the offending provider, instead of a clear validation error naming the grant.

adjudication.rationale: In `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit`, the code does `String grantShortcut = gtf.getShortcut();` and immediately calls `grantsByShortcuts.put(grantShortcut, grantName)` / `grantsToShortcuts.put(grantName, grantShortcut)` with `grantsByShortcuts` and `grantsToShortcuts` being `ConcurrentHashMap`s. `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids null keys/values, so any `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` implementation returning `null` from `getShortcut()` will trigger a `NullPointerException` during server `postInit` (startup), with no explicit validation/error message identifying the offending provider. The diff adds `getShortcut()` but does not enforce non-null in the interface or validate it in `postInit`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The lazy shortcut-map refresh in getShortcutByGrantType writes to grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts concurrently from request threads via ConcurrentHashMap, but the duplicate-shortcut invariant checked once in postInit (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()) is never re-validated on the lazy path, and a newly hot-deployed grant reusing an existing shortcut silently overwrites the earlier mapping. After a hot deploy of a grant with a colliding shortcut, tokens minted under one grant type decode as the other grant type — silently wrong token context reported to any consumer of getTokenContextFromTokenId, with no error logged or thrown.

adjudication.rationale: In `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.getShortcutByGrantType`, the lazy refresh path (when `grantsToShortcuts.get(grantType)` is null) loads a newly available `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` and then does `grantsByShortcuts.put(shortcut, grantType)` / `grantsToShortcuts.put(grantType, shortcut)` without any collision/uniqueness validation. This can silently overwrite an existing `grantsByShortcuts` entry if the new hot-deployed grant reuses an existing shortcut, while leaving the old `grantsToShortcuts` entry intact. The only duplicate-shortcut check (`if (grantsByShortcuts.size() != grantsToShortcuts.size()) throw ...`) exists only in `postInit` and is not re-run on the lazy path, so a colliding shortcut introduced after startup can corrupt the mapping and cause `getTokenContextFromTokenId()` to decode the wrong grant type with no error.
